1303.title: Guidelines
1303.hook: seventh point: do everything with one intention; begin and end the day with it
1303.howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training often set the wish to benefit others on waking and review the day before sleep, rejoicing in what went well and regretting what did not, then renewing the intention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the commitments of the sixth point. Your line: don't wait in ambush.

Before your feet hit the floor this morning, what was the first thing in your head? A deadline. A phone. Last night's argument. And the last thing at night is often whatever happened to be on the screen. Both ends of the day get handed to whatever shows up first. The seventh and last point of mind training, lojong, takes those two moments back on purpose. Its guidelines are short, and one is almost too simple to notice: do everything with one intention, and begin and end the day with it.
screen: `THE FIRST THOUGHT OF THE DAY.` → `THE LAST ONE.` → `THE SEVENTH POINT TAKES THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: First, what the guidelines are: short lines for ordinary life, after the cushion. Not special practice; the dishes, the inbox, the commute. Second, one intention. A line usually given as: do all activities with one intention. Teachers explain the intention as bodhicitta, the wish to wake up for the sake of others, the same wish all of mind training has been growing. One thread runs through everything, so typing an email and sitting in meditation become the same work, done for the same reason. Third, two activities, one at the beginning and one at the end. In the morning, set the intention before the day sets it for you. At night, look back. Teachers describe the evening as a gentle review: be glad for what went well, be honest about what didn't, and set the intention again for tomorrow. No punishment in it, just a clear look and a fresh start. Fourth, steadiness. Another line of point seven is usually given as: whichever of the two occurs, be patient. Commentaries read the two as good fortune and bad. Neither a good day nor a hard one is a reason to drop the thread. The point isn't a perfect day; it's that the thread holds either way. And with that, the seven points credited to Chekawa are complete: the basics, the main practice, trouble as the path, a whole life's practice, checking yourself, commitments, and now guidelines. Tomorrow the block turns from training the mind to bringing the body down to the floor.
screen: `SHORT LINES FOR ORDINARY LIFE.` · `ONE INTENTION, ONE THREAD.` · `ONE AT THE START, ONE AT THE END.` · `PATIENT, GOOD DAY OR BAD.` · then, large: `ONE INTENTION.`

segments.voice: Run back over the day so far, the way the evening review does: find one moment you're glad of and stay with it a breath, then one that didn't go well, and see it plainly, without scolding. Then put one intention into a few plain words for what's left of the day, something like: to be of use to someone. Hold it gently while you breathe.
Guidelines. The seventh point of mind training: everything done with one intention, set in the morning and renewed at night. Today's word.
Your line: one intention. Set in the morning, looked back on at night. See you tomorrow.

1304.title: Prostrations
1304.hook: full-length bows, done by the hundred and thousand
1304.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists do full-length prostrations in temples, shrine rooms and on pilgrimage, often reciting refuge while they bow, and as part of the foundational practices students complete them in large numbers over months or years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guidelines, and the seven points complete. Your line: one intention.

There's a kind of bow that leaves nothing standing. Palms come together. The knees go down, the hands slide forward along the ground, and the whole body lies flat, forehead to the floor, arms stretched ahead. A breath. Then all of it reverses, back to standing. And then, in temples and quiet shrine rooms in Tibetan Buddhist communities, people do it again, and again. Some keep a pair of smooth wooden boards under their hands so they can slide. Back on day two, you bowed three times, to the three jewels. Today, the bow that uses the whole body.
screen: `A BOW THAT LEAVES NOTHING STANDING.` → `FLAT ON THE GROUND, ARMS AHEAD.` → `AND THEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, how it's done. In Tibetan teachings the joined palms often touch three places before the body goes down: the crown, the throat, the heart. Teachers link them to body, speech and mind, so the bow is the whole person, offered. Second, why the body. Pride is something you can feel in your posture: chest out, chin up, standing over things. A full prostration is the body doing the opposite, on purpose. Teachers call it a remedy for pride, and say the mind tends to follow where the body goes. Third, by the hundred and the thousand. In the Tibetan foundational practices, which tomorrow opens up, prostrations are done together with taking refuge, the turn met earlier with the lamrim. Practitioners picture the Buddha, the teaching and the community in front of them, and bow to them. Tradition sets a very large number, and people work through it over months or years, a session at a time. Some pilgrims even travel by prostration, measuring a road with the length of their own bodies. Fourth, all the way down. A half bow stops where it's comfortable. This one goes to the floor, where there's no further to fall. Then it gets up. Teachers point out that rising matters as much as going down: you return to standing, lighter, and begin again.
screen: `CROWN, THROAT, HEART.` · `THE BODY UNDOES PRIDE.` · `BOWED WITH REFUGE, OVER AND OVER.` · `TO THE FLOOR, AND UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: If your body allows it, do three prostrations on a clear patch of floor: palms to crown, throat and heart, then kneel, slide your hands forward, lie flat for one breath, and come back up slowly. If a full bow isn't right for your knees or your back, kneel and bow your forehead toward the floor, or simply bow your head where you sit. Then rest in the stillness after the third.
Prostrations. Full-length bows, the whole body to the ground, done over and over in Tibetan practice. Today's word.
Your line: all the way down. And all the way up again. Day thirteen-oh-four, done.

1305.title: The foundations
1305.hook: the preliminary practices: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga
1305.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist students complete the ngondro under a teacher's guidance, doing refuge with prostrations, Vajrasattva purification, the mandala offering and guru yoga, often over years and alongside ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prostrations, the whole body to the ground. Your line: all the way down.

Nobody stops on the sidewalk to admire a foundation. It's poured first, it's underground, and soon it's covered with floors and furniture. But build a house without one and the house will tell you. Doors stick. Cracks run up the walls. Tibetan Buddhism has a name for the work that goes under everything else, the part nobody photographs and some practitioners spend years on. Yesterday's bow was the first piece of it. Today's word is the whole foundation: ngondro.
screen: `NOBODY ADMIRES A FOUNDATION.` → `WITHOUT ONE, THE HOUSE TELLS YOU.` → `NGONDRO.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ngondro is Tibetan, usually translated the preliminaries: the practices that come before the deeper meditations a teacher may give later. But before doesn't mean less. Second, the four. Refuge and prostration: going to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, with the body bowing all the way down. Purification: the mantra of Vajrasattva, for washing away past wrongs. The mandala offering: giving away the whole world, pictured on a plate of rice. And guru yoga: joining your mind with the teacher's awakened mind. Each gets its own day this week; today is just the map. Third, schools build it differently. In some lineages the ngondro opens with four thoughts that turn the mind, the same four that opened mind training last week: the preciousness of a human life, impermanence, karma, and the suffering of the round. Other schools arrange their preliminaries in their own order, with their own lists. Tradition sets each practice at a large number of repetitions, and people often complete them slowly, around jobs and families, over a long time. Fourth, why the foundation matters so much. A saying heard in Tibetan teaching puts it boldly: the preliminaries are more profound than the main practice. Some teachers go back to them again and again, long after finishing. A foundation isn't the part you outgrow. It's the part everything else stands on.
screen: `NGONDRO: WHAT COMES BEFORE.` · `REFUGE, PURIFICATION, OFFERING, GURU.` · `SCHOOLS BUILD IT DIFFERENTLY.` · `NOT OUTGROWN, STOOD ON.` · then, large: `THE FOUNDATIONS.`

segments.voice: Picture a plain square slab of foundation, seen from above, and set one practice at each corner as you breathe: refuge and prostration, purification, the offering, guru yoga. Walk around the square once more, slower, letting each one sit for a moment; you don't need to do any of them, just know where each one stands. Then rest in the plain breath under it, the way a house rests on what's underneath.
Ngondro. The preliminaries, the foundations of Tibetan practice: refuge and prostration, purification, offering, guru yoga. Today's word.
Your line: the foundations. Quiet work, poured first, and holding up everything else. Until tomorrow.

1306.title: The mandala offering
1306.hook: offering the whole universe, pictured as a mandala of rice
1306.howItsDone: In the Tibetan foundational practices, students build and offer a mandala of rice on a round plate many times while reciting an offering verse, picturing the whole universe given to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ngondro, the four practices under everything else. Your line: the foundations.

A small round plate, often brass or silver. A bowl of rice beside it. The practitioner wipes the plate in circles with the inside of the wrist, then lets rice fall in a ring, sets a smaller ring on top, then another, until there's a little stacked heap with an ornament on top. A verse is recited. Then the rice is tipped off, the plate wiped, and it all begins again. From across the room it could pass for a child's game with dinner. In the practitioner's mind, it's the whole universe, being given away.
screen: `A PLATE, A BOWL OF RICE.` → `RINGS ON RINGS.` → `TIPPED OFF, BEGUN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Mandala is a Sanskrit word usually translated circle. Here the circle is the world itself, ordered and complete, seen from above. Second, what the rice stands for. The offering draws on a picture of the cosmos found in Buddhist texts from India: at the center a great mountain, Meru; around it continents and oceans, a sun and a moon, and every precious thing anyone could want. Each heap of rice stands in for a part of that world, so the little plate holds mountains, oceans and everything between. Third, why give the universe away. None of it is yours, and that's partly the point. Teachers explain the offering as a training in generosity with no ceiling. People often give what they can spare; here the practitioner gives everything, beautiful things included, along with their own body and their own good deeds. Tibetan teachers count it among the ways of gathering merit, the goodness that ripens into a path. What gets lighter is the grip. Fourth, wiping the plate. Some teachers say the wiping is as much the practice as the heaping: clearing the mind the way you clear the plate. And when the rice is tipped off, nothing is kept. Offered, emptied, offered again. In year one you met the sand mandala some monasteries build and sweep away. This one shares the word, but it's a gift you can carry in two hands.
screen: `MANDALA: A CIRCLE, THE WORLD.` · `MOUNTAIN, CONTINENTS, SUN AND MOON.` · `GIVING WITHOUT A CEILING.` · `WIPED, EMPTIED, OFFERED AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your lap, palms up, and bring to mind one thing complete and good in your world: a morning, a view, a person's laugh, the light in a window. Let it sit in your open hands the way the rice sits on the plate, then give it away, and let your hands stay open after. If you are a Buddhist, you can offer it to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.
The mandala offering. The whole universe, pictured in heaps of rice on a round plate, and given away. Today's word.
Your line: the whole world offered. Held in two hands, then let go. Same time tomorrow.

1307.title: Purification
1307.hook: the hundred-syllable mantra of Vajrasattva, for purifying past wrongs
1307.howItsDone: In the Tibetan foundational practices, students recite Vajrasattva's hundred-syllable mantra many times while visualizing purifying nectar, relying on the four powers of regret, reliance, remedy and resolve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mandala offering, the universe in heaps of rice. Your line: the whole world offered.

"He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." That's the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation. Tradition links the verse to Angulimala, the feared bandit you met back in year one, who met the Buddha and became a monk. The verse doesn't say the moon was never dim. It says clouds pass, and light comes back. Tibetan practice has a whole method for those clouds, for things a person has done and can't undo. It's the second of the four foundations, and it centers on a figure in white.
screen: `LIKE THE MOON FREED FROM CLOUDS.` → `THE CLOUDS PASS.` → `A FIGURE IN WHITE.`

segments.voice: First, Vajrasattva. In the practice texts he's pictured seated above the practitioner's head, white as moonlight, holding a vajra and a bell. His name is usually rendered something like diamond being, and Tibetan teachers present him as the purity of all the buddhas in one form. Second, the mantra. His long hundred-syllable mantra is recited again and again while the practitioner pictures bright nectar pouring down from him, through the crown, filling the body. Old wrongs and harms leave as dark liquid, washed down and out. Third, the four powers. Gampopa and other Tibetan teachers say purification rests on four supports: honest regret for what was done, reliance on refuge and on the wish to help others, the remedy itself, like the mantra, and the resolve not to do it again. Notice what isn't on the list: punishing yourself. Regret here means seeing clearly, not sinking. Fourth, washed clean. In versions of the practice, Vajrasattva declares at the end that the practitioner's wrongs are purified, then dissolves into light that melts into them. Teachers explain the logic with a picture close to the Dhammapada's: the stains are like clouds, not the moon itself. The mind underneath, they say, was never ruined. In their telling, purification doesn't erase the past. It loosens the past's grip on the present, so a person can stand in the light again and choose differently.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you wish you hadn't done, not the worst thing, just a real one, and look at it honestly for a moment, without arguing and without punishing. Then picture something clear and cool pouring down over you, like water or light, and let the heaviness run out with each breath out. At the end, quietly make one small resolve about what you'd do differently.
Purification. In the Tibetan foundations, Vajrasattva's practice: honest regret, a remedy, and resolve, until the clouds pass. Today's word.
Your line: washed clean. Clouds pass, and the moon was never ruined. See you tomorrow.

1308.title: Guru yoga
1308.hook: joining one's mind with the teacher's awakened mind
1308.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists practice guru yoga as the culmination of the foundational practices and often daily afterward, visualizing the teacher as an awakened figure such as Padmasambhava or Tsongkhapa, receiving blessings and resting with the mind joined to the teacher's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purification, and the moon freed from clouds. Your line: washed clean.

A kid stands at a kitchen counter beside a grandmother making bread. No recipe card. The kid watches her hands and copies them, badly at first, for years. Decades later, that kid is kneading dough and notices: these are her hands. Same push, same fold, same little slap at the end. Nobody taught it in words. It passed across, from one person to another, by being close. Tibetan Buddhism has a practice built on that kind of closeness, the last of the four foundations.
screen: `A KID AT A KITCHEN COUNTER.` → `THESE ARE HER HANDS.` → `IT PASSED ACROSS, BY CLOSENESS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Guru is Sanskrit for teacher; in Tibetan, lama. Teachers often explain yoga here as joining, so guru yoga is joining with the teacher. Second, who is pictured. The practitioner visualizes the teacher, usually not as an ordinary person but as an awakened figure from the lineage. In Nyingma practice it's often Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche. In Gelug practice, a well-known guru yoga centers on Tsongkhapa. The figure appears in the sky ahead, or above the head, bright and kind. Third, receiving. In versions of the practice, light streams from the teacher's forehead, throat and heart to the practitioner's own: body, speech and mind, the same three the prostrations linked to crown, throat and heart. The student asks for blessing and receives it as light. Fourth, joining. At the end, the teacher melts into light and dissolves into the practitioner, who rests with no separation between the two minds. Tibetan teachers explain that what's joined isn't a personality. It's the awakened mind the teacher stands for, which they say is the student's own nature too. And one caution from inside the tradition, the one you met in year one: check the teacher. Tibetan texts on the path advise examining a teacher carefully, for a long time, before placing this kind of trust. Guru yoga rests on a teacher's real goodness. It isn't meant to ask anyone to set their judgment aside.
screen: `GURU, LAMA: THE TEACHER.` · `PICTURED AS AN AWAKENED FIGURE.` · `LIGHT TO BODY, SPEECH AND MIND.` · `DISSOLVING: ONE MIND.` · then, large: `JOINING MINDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something good, a teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a friend, a writer you never met, and picture them a little above and in front of you. Let one quality of theirs come forward: their patience, their honesty, the way they listened. Breathing in, let that quality come toward you like light; breathing out, let it settle in, until it feels less like theirs and more like yours.
Guru yoga. Joining with the teacher: picturing them, receiving their blessing, and resting as one awakened mind. Today's word.
Your line: joining minds. Some things pass across only by being close. Day thirteen-oh-eight, done.

1309.title: Deity yoga, explained
1309.hook: visualizing oneself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous
1309.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners take up deity yoga after receiving empowerment and instruction from a teacher, typically meditating daily with a practice text in which they arise as the deity from emptiness and recite the deity's mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, guru yoga, the last of the four foundations. Your line: joining minds.

What comes up when you picture yourself? For some people it's someone a little tired, a little behind, with a list of flaws ready to recite. A picture like that can run all day, mostly unnoticed, shaping what seems possible. Tibetan tantric Buddhism does something bold with that habit. It doesn't argue with the old picture. It replaces it, on purpose, for the length of a meditation, with the picture of an awakened being. To an outsider it can look like pretending. Today, what it actually is.
screen: `THE PICTURE YOU CARRY OF YOURSELF.` → `IT RUNS ALL DAY.` → `REPLACE IT, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, what deity yoga is. In Vajrayana, the diamond vehicle you met in year one, the practitioner visualizes themselves as an awakened figure, such as Tara or Avalokiteshvara, with a body made of light and the surroundings as a pure land. The deity isn't a god to be pleased from a distance. It's a form of awakening itself. Second, empty and luminous. The practice usually begins by letting the ordinary self-image dissolve into emptiness. Then the deity arises out of it, clear and vivid, but without solid substance, like a rainbow or a reflection in a mirror. Teachers call that the guardrail. If the figure were solid, they say, this would just be a fancier ego. Because it's understood as empty, it loosens the grip of every self-image, the old one included. Third, two qualities Tibetan teachers name: clear appearance, seeing the form vividly, and what's often called divine pride, a steady confidence of being awakened that isn't the ego's pride at all. Fourth, how it's learned. In Tibetan traditions, full deity yoga is practiced after receiving empowerment and instruction from a qualified teacher, usually on top of the foundations you met this week. So this is an explanation, not the practice. Each of this week's steps, one intention, all the way down, the foundations, the whole world offered, washed clean, joining minds, clears ground, so that seeing yourself as awakened rests on something real.
screen: `YOURSELF AS AN AWAKENED FIGURE.` · `ARISING FROM EMPTINESS, LIKE A RAINBOW.` · `CLEAR APPEARANCE, DIVINE PRIDE.` · `LEARNED WITH EMPOWERMENT AND A TEACHER.` · then, large: `AS THE DEITY.`

segments.voice: This isn't deity yoga, just a small taste of the idea, open to anyone: let your usual picture of yourself soften, the list and the flaws, like mist thinning. Then picture yourself made of kindness, clear as a reflection, with nothing solid to defend, and feel how that body would sit and breathe. When the old picture returns, let it pass like weather.
Deity yoga. Seeing yourself as an awakened figure, understood as empty and luminous, like a rainbow. Today's word.
Your line: as the deity. Clear as a rainbow, with nothing solid to defend. Rest well.
